interactions.label: During the forensic examination of a poisoning victim, which agent is identified

params.question: During the forensic examination of a poisoning victim, which agent is identified by blue-black staining of the oral mucosa?

answers.text: Copper sulphate

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Copper sulphate produces brilliant blue crystals and causes blue-green vomitus, which is essentially pathognomonic — but it does not cause blue-black mucosal staining.

answers.text: Yellow phosphorus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Yellow phosphorus is waxy and pale, with a characteristic garlic odour and phosphorescent glow. It does not cause blue-black staining of the mucosa.

answers.text: Iodine

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Iodine leaves characteristic blue-black staining on the mucous membranes, making it readily identifiable on oral examination during forensic assessment.

answers.text: Arsenic trioxide

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Arsenic trioxide is a fine white powder easily mistaken for flour or sugar. It produces a garlic-like odour but does not cause blue-black mucosal staining.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the colour clues: copper sulphate → blue-green vomitus, phosphorus → pale waxy substance with phosphorescent glow, arsenic → white powder, and iodine → blue-black mucosal staining.
Well done. Colour-based identification is one of the first diagnostic tools in forensic toxicology — iodine's blue-black staining is virtually diagnostic.

interactions.label: A farmer is brought to the emergency department 36 hours after ingesting yellow

params.question: A farmer is brought to the emergency department 36 hours after ingesting yellow phosphorus. He currently appears to be recovering, with resolving nausea and no vomiting. His anxious relatives offer him milk. What is the most appropriate course of action?

answers.text: Allow the milk — it will soothe the damaged gastric mucosa

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Milk and all fatty foods are absolutely contraindicated in phosphorus poisoning. Phosphorus is highly fat-soluble, and fats dramatically increase its absorption. Magnesium sulphate is the correct purgative.

answers.text: Refuse the milk and continue close monitoring for impending hepatorenal failure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. This patient is in phase 2 — the deceptive latent period — where symptoms temporarily ease. Phase 3 (hepatorenal failure with fatty liver degeneration) follows. Milk is contraindicated because phosphorus is fat-soluble, and fats increase absorption.

answers.text: Discharge the patient with instructions to return if symptoms recur

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Discharging during the latent phase is dangerous. Phase 2 of phosphorus poisoning mimics recovery, but phase 3 — liver failure, acute kidney injury, and cardiovascular collapse — typically follows within days.

answers.text: Perform gastric lavage with sodium thiosulphate

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Sodium thiosulphate is used for iodine poisoning, not phosphorus. Copper sulphate lavage is the traditional decontamination for phosphorus. Additionally, gastric lavage at 36 hours post-ingestion is unlikely to yield benefit.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: phosphorus poisoning follows three phases — GI irritation, deceptive latent period, then hepatorenal failure. Fats (milk, castor oil) are absolutely contraindicated because phosphorus is fat-soluble.
Excellent. Recognising the deceptive latent period and avoiding fats are two critical principles in phosphorus poisoning management that directly affect survival.

interactions.label: A 3-year-old child presents with haematemesis after accidentally ingesting iron

params.question: A 3-year-old child presents with haematemesis after accidentally ingesting iron tablets. The treating physician considers chelation therapy. Which chelating agent is specifically contraindicated?

answers.text: Deferoxamine

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Deferoxamine is the specific chelator for iron poisoning. Vin rosé–coloured urine confirms that it is working effectively.

answers.text: Calcium EDTA

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Calcium EDTA is the chelator for lead poisoning. It is not indicated for iron, but it does not carry the specific danger that BAL does.

answers.text: D-penicillamine

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: D-penicillamine is used for copper poisoning. While not the agent of choice for iron, it does not carry the specific contraindication that BAL does.

answers.text: Dimercaprol (BAL)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. BAL is absolutely contraindicated in iron poisoning. It forms a fat-soluble iron–BAL complex that redistributes into the central nervous system, worsening toxicity rather than relieving it. Deferoxamine is the correct chelator.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the chelation rules: deferoxamine for iron, dimercaprol (BAL) for arsenic and mercury, calcium EDTA for lead, D-penicillamine for copper. BAL is specifically contraindicated in iron because the iron–BAL complex is fat-soluble and enters the CNS.
Well done. The BAL contraindication in iron poisoning is an absolute rule — the fat-soluble iron–BAL complex crosses into the CNS and worsens toxicity.

interactions.label: While examining an unconscious patient suspected of poisoning, you note pinpoint

params.question: While examining an unconscious patient suspected of poisoning, you note pinpoint pupils and a garlic-like odour on the breath. Gastric lavage has already been started by the casualty team. Which specimen action should you prioritise?

answers.text: Collect fifty millilitres of urine in a sterile container

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Urine collection is important but comes after gastric specimens and blood in the priority order. With lavage already started, the gastric washings are the most time-sensitive specimen.

answers.text: Draw blood in a grey-topped fluoride-oxalate tube

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The fluoride-oxalate tube is correct for ethanol and volatile substances. However, since lavage has already begun, the first 200 mL of washings must be secured immediately — this specimen is being lost with every passing moment.

answers.text: Collect the first 200 millilitres of lavage washings in a sealed glass bottle

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The pre-lavage gastric aspirate — the highest-priority specimen — has been lost. The first 200 millilitres of lavage washings are the next best sample and must be collected immediately in a sealed glass bottle before they are discarded.

answers.text: Request hair and nail clippings for chronic exposure analysis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Hair and nail clippings can document chronic exposure (e.g., Mees' lines in arsenic poisoning) but are not time-sensitive. The lavage washings, which are actively being generated and may be discarded, take priority.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the specimen priority: gastric aspirate first (sealed glass bottle, before lavage), then blood (fluoride-oxalate for volatiles), then urine, then vomitus. If lavage has already begun, keep the first 200 mL of washings.
Good. In forensic practice, the gastric specimen is the highest priority and is time-limited. When the first aspirate has been lost to lavage, salvaging the initial washings is critical.

interactions.label: A patient presents with rapidly ascending flaccid paralysis and a serum potassiu

params.question: A patient presents with rapidly ascending flaccid paralysis and a serum potassium of 1.8 mEq/L. Total body potassium is estimated to be normal. Which mechanism best explains this presentation?

answers.text: Massive renal potassium wasting due to tubular injury

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Renal wasting would reduce total body potassium, but here total body potassium is normal. This pattern — low serum K⁺ with normal total body K⁺ — indicates intracellular redistribution, not renal loss.

answers.text: Blockade of potassium channels trapping potassium intracellularly

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. This is the hallmark of soluble barium poisoning. Barium ions block inward-rectifier potassium channels, trapping potassium inside cells. Plasma potassium falls sharply despite normal total body potassium, producing ascending flaccid paralysis that can mimic Guillain-Barré syndrome. Treatment is intravenous potassium chloride.

answers.text: Inhibition of the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump preventing potassium uptake into cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Inhibiting the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase would cause potassium to leak OUT of cells (as the pump normally moves K⁺ into cells), raising serum potassium — the opposite of what is seen here.

answers.text: Gastrointestinal potassium loss from profuse diarrhoea

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: GI losses (as seen in cholera or arsenic poisoning) would deplete total body potassium. In this patient, total body potassium is normal, pointing to a redistribution mechanism rather than true depletion.

overallFeedback.feedback: The critical clue is normal total body potassium with very low serum potassium. This rules out losses (renal or GI) and points to intracellular trapping — the mechanism of soluble barium salts blocking potassium channels.
Excellent analysis. The key insight is that barium causes redistributive — not depletional — hypokalaemia. Low serum K⁺ with normal total body K⁺ is virtually diagnostic of soluble barium poisoning.
